title: Active Graph Agent Runtime (BabyAGI 4) — Yohei Nakajima, Untapped Capital

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses

summary: Nakajima introduces ActiveGraph as an experimental, open-source event-sourced graph runtime where the immutable event log—not the LLM—is the core unit of agent construction. Every action and every change to the agent flattens into a single typed log that projects a graph as the agent's state. Behaviors react to graph changes and emit events; policies govern which changes are autonomous, need human approval, or require contradiction checks. Views provide context management as graph queries. Object schemas, tools, deterministic and LLM behaviors, and pack policies assemble into modular packs (core, tool, secret, memory, identity, communication, chat) that combine to form agent harnesses. LLMs never talk directly to each other—they communicate only through shared state, inspired by blackboard systems from the 1970s and Kafka-style micro-workers. The architecture yields native replays, rollbacks, and forks, and Nakajima notes it is unintuitive for humans but AI coding assistants handle it well. Using the structured log itself as memory performed competitively on LongMemEval, where an API key failure at question 350 rolled back one step and resumed at 353. Reference agents (coding via Replit, deep research) built natively on ActiveGraph produced event logs and evidence graphs without explicit design. Nakajima then explores self-improvement: a project called Regimes classifies failures, allows the agent to edit specific parts of itself, runs sandbox gate checks, and only accepts changes that improve accuracy—yielding modest but statistically significant gains on LongMemEval. ActiveGraph Lab reads his blog posts, proposes and runs experiments, found a bug in its own code, wrote and merged a PR, and discovered packs are modular across repos. A Pokemon card Kaggle competition served as a testbed where 80 experimental passes, each gated by simulated games and win-rate thresholds, accepted about 20-30 changes and improved the score while tracking what didn't work. Surprises include AI being better at architecting these agents (decades of training data on event-sourced shared-state patterns), debugging shifting from session logs to the ActiveGraph DB, and packs loading from other repos. Nakajima hypothesizes that long-running agents need an experiential world model—an immutable event log projecting state, analogous to the hippocampus—alongside predictive world models, suggesting the harness will not disappear as models improve.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and three years of BabyAGI
sections.summary: Nakajima introduces himself as a VC and builder, recounts the original BabyAGI launch in March 2023 and its viral reception, and describes nine subsequent iterations focused on self-improvement. He traces his recurring use of graphs across projects and introduces ActiveGraph as an event-sourced graph runtime for auditable agents.

sections.title: Build around the log, not the LLM
sections.summary: Nakajima contrasts LLM-centric agent building with log-centric building. In ActiveGraph, every action and change flattens into a single immutable event log that projects a graph as agent state. LLMs communicate through shared state, not directly. This yields native replays, rollbacks, and forks. He notes it is a runtime, not a harness, and common harnesses can be rebuilt on top.

sections.title: Behaviors, policies, and views
sections.summary: Behaviors listen to graph changes and emit events; a planner behavior adds task and relationship objects on goal creation. Behavior subscriptions can be complex graph queries, such as triggering a contradiction detector. Views provide context management as graph queries. Policies determine which changes require proposed patches, human approval, or contradiction checks.

sections.title: Packs and blackboard architecture lineage
sections.summary: Object schemas, tools, deterministic and LLM behaviors assemble into modular packs with pack policies, forming harnesses on ActiveGraph. Nakajima compares the architecture to blackboard systems from the 1970s/80s and Kafka-style micro-workers communicating through shared state. A ReAct agent rebuilt on ActiveGraph demonstrates common harnesses work on the runtime.

sections.title: Log as memory and the API key that resumed itself
sections.summary: Nakajima experiments with using the structured log itself as memory—leveraging the log's ordering plus embedding of messages. On LongMemEval, this performed well without semantic ingestion or entity extraction. During a 500-question run, his API key ran out at question 350; upon refreshing, the agent rolled back one step and resumed at 353.

sections.title: Reference agents built natively on the log
sections.summary: Reference agents built on ActiveGraph include a coding agent via Replit that natively produced an event log graph and a deep research agent that natively produced an event log with evidence and contradiction graphs. These features emerged without explicit planning. Nakajima begins introducing ActiveGraph packs as a step toward more complete agent systems.

sections.title: Packs overview and self-improvement: Regimes
sections.summary: Nakajima enumerates packs (core, tool, secret, memory, identity, communication, chat) that bundle object types, behaviors, and policies; packs are swappable and combine to form agents. He then introduces Regimes, a controlled self-modification project: the agent runs ~20 questions, classifies failures, edits specific parts of itself, tests on 50 questions, and accepts changes only if accuracy rises. Loops ran 8-13 times, accepting 4-5 patches, with modest but statistically significant LongMemEval improvement. The agent also tracked what did not work.

sections.title: ActiveGraph Lab writes its own experiments
sections.summary: ActiveGraph Lab reads all of Nakajima's blog posts and GitHub repos, proposes new ideas, asks permission to run experiments, and writes blog posts about results. It found a bug in its own code, asked to fix it, wrote and merged a PR. It also installed a pack from another repo and wrote a blog post discovering cross-repo pack modularity, surprising Nakajima.

sections.title: A Pokemon card competition as a testbed
sections.summary: Nakajima entered a Kaggle Pokemon trading card deck competition with deterministic Elo-style battles. Using ActiveGraph, he ran ~80 experimental passes, each gated by ~200 simulated games against three reference agents with win-rate and Wilson score thresholds. About 20-30 changes were accepted, improving the score to ~27%. The agent tracked failed experiments, a contrast from YOLO agents that only remember successes.

sections.title: Surprises: why AI architects this better
sections.summary: Nakajima lists pleasant surprises: AI seems better at architecting log-based agents, likely because event-sourced shared-state patterns (Kafka, blackboard) have decades of training data versus only ~3 years for LLM-agent patterns. Debugging shifted from session logs to querying the ActiveGraph DB. Packs loaded from other repos without extra work. No more restarting long runs from scratch, and failed experiments are tracked.

sections.title: Why an agent needs an experiential world model
sections.summary: Nakajima hypothesizes that long-running agents need not just a predictive world model (priors) but an experiential world model—an immutable event log projecting state, analogous to the hippocampus, which replays and feeds state back into priors. He argues the harness will not disappear as models improve, and that agent identity should be derived from its own log, much as human identity derives from life experience. He invites listeners to try ActiveGraph.

demonstrations: ReAct agent rebuilt on ActiveGraph: goal-created triggers a thought, thought-created triggers the reason function, showing common harnesses can be reconstructed on the runtime.
Log-as-memory experiment on LongMemEval: embedded queries, retrieved relevant messages with context window before and after, no semantic ingestion or entity extraction, achieving competitive results.
Coding agent built by Replit on ActiveGraph natively produced an event log graph.
Deep research agent built on ActiveGraph natively produced an event log and evidence/contradiction graph.

Regimes self-improvement loop: agent runs ~20 questions, self-modifies, tests on 50 questions, accepts changes only if accuracy rises; looped 8-13 times accepting 4-5 patches with modest but statistically significant LongMemEval gains.

ActiveGraph Lab reads blog posts, proposes and runs experiments, found a bug in its own code and wrote/merged a PR, and installed a pack from another repo and wrote a blog post about cross-repo modularity.

Pokemon card Kaggle competition: 80 experimental passes, each running ~200 simulated games against three reference agents with win-rate and Wilson score thresholds; accepted ~20-30 changes, improving Elo score to ~27%.
limitations: ActiveGraph is described as experimental and intended to inspire new ideas rather than serve as a production framework.
The architecture is unintuitive for humans to write directly; Nakajima says he would never write the code himself.
Log-as-memory experiment did not include semantic ingestion, fact extraction, or entity extraction; improvements were possible but Nakajima moved on.
Nakajima caveats that he does not know how to train models; the experiential world model is a hypothesis, not a proven claim.
Pokemon card score plateaued around 27%; unclear if further improvement is possible.
